### Historical audit: S0067

**Source:** `/srv/lab-disks/disk2/users/xymo/Documents/Codex/2026-11-02/scene-rsi-rsi-1-3d-blender/outputs/scene_rsi_pilot/results/ablation_r1/ours_without_probes/C1/test/commons_155212263/trajectory.jsonl`. Citations below refer to its JSONL lines; the supplied observations are whole lines, not split fragments.

| Evidence | Observed operations and limits |
|---|---|
| Goal — lines 1, 3 | The task requested an editable reconstruction from one photograph. The student **interpreted** it as a historic metalworking workshop and estimated image anchors and an oblique camera. The image itself is not available in this audit, so that interpretation is not independently verified. |
| Initial build and audit — lines 3–7 | The draft specified multiple benches, lathes, flywheels, an anvil, containers and architecture, with separate assets and colored wood, iron, rust and glazing. A controller source-audit prompt requested checks, not a visual diagnosis. The next student program adopted dimension/key assertions, separate pose parameters, subtree traversal and material copying; that program was sent to Blender. Source grouping and intended support coordinates do not establish physical contact. |
| Failure and revision — lines 8–12 | Step 1 timed out after 600 seconds, with empty logs and no image. The student hypothesized that complexity was a problem and reduced floor subdivisions, tube sampling, bucket panels and material copies while retaining the camera and broad layout. The revised code was executed. The timeout alone does not identify its cause, nor does the subsequent success isolate which change mattered. |
| Validation and interruption — lines 13–18 | Step 2 returned `ok: true`, saved a render and scene, and was selected. The render and reference were supplied to a subsequent student call, but that call timed out and produced no recorded response; the scene loop then reported an error. Thus there is a successful build/render and selected step, but no visible completed comparison, final correctness verdict or confirmed final submission. This is a technical interruption, not an empty patch or established algorithmic failure. |

**Scene checks.** The executed source describes multiple independent objects, colored materials and geometric floorboard variation, but no external texture maps. It specifies articulated-looking machine parts, angled papers and leaning tools, a camera, world illumination and three area lights (lines 11–12). These establish intended construction and pose, not verified connections, contacts, framing, texture fidelity or lighting quality. The saved render’s pixels are not supplied here; neither visual similarity nor cropping and occlusion can be assessed independently.

**Teacher and exploration.** No teacher agent or teacher diagnosis appears in this student trajectory. The source-audit and execution-failure messages were actual controller inputs, and the subsequent code demonstrates response to them; they should not be recast as teacher findings. The student independently chose the initial scene interpretation and the simplification strategy. No diagnostic probes or additional autonomous tool exploration are recorded; the relevant CLI sessions report zero tool calls (lines 2, 5, 10, 16).

**Lessons and uncertainty.** Transferably, a failed render should not be treated as visual evidence, and a simpler production build can recover a render under a time limit. Task-specific choices—workshop inventory, poses and camera—remain hypotheses. In particular, whether complexity caused the first timeout, whether the selected scene matches the photograph, and whether its assembled parts truly contact their supports remain unresolved.
